description:
Hi, I'm Vanishree, leading team NEBULYX on Flame in Freefall. We're building PyroMorph, an AI tool that uses NASA's microgravity combustion data to predict whether a flame survives or goes out based on oxygen level and airflow, shown in an interactive dashboard.
Looking for: Python/data analysis, machine learning, dashboard or front-end skills, and someone good at research or pitching. Beginners who are eager to learn are welcome!
summary: In microgravity, buoyant convection disappears, so flames become slow, round and controlled by diffusion and heat loss. This is a major spacecraft fire-safety concern, but the real experimental data is hard for non-specialists to explore. We built an interactive web lab for the Flame in Freefall challenge, using 83 published ISS runs from NASA’s BASS-II dataset, drawn from Zhao et al. (2015) and Link et al. (2018). Users adjust oxygen level (16 to 21%) and forced airflow (0.5 to 10 cm/s) and see a live visual of how the flame responds, including the quench edge where flames die out at about 2 to 5 cm/s in the fabric tests. A Compare view lets users set scenarios side by side. The project is built on one rule: it shows only what was measured, with zero AI extrapolation, and a Sources & Limits section states where the evidence stops. This makes real combustion science accessible, transparent and easy to verify.
details:
Ignis Atelier – Exploring Fire Beyond Earth

We built Ignis Atelier with one simple question in mind: What actually happens to fire in space?

On Earth, hot air rises and helps keep a flame burning. But in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, things work differently. Without normal buoyancy, flames can become slower, rounder, and behave in ways we rarely get to observe on Earth.

We wanted to make these unusual fire behaviours easier for everyone to understand, so we created an interactive lab using real experimental data.

Our project is based on 83 published ISS experimental runs from NASA's BASS-II dataset, including research by Zhao et al. (2015) and Link et al. (2018). Instead of simply displaying graphs and scientific results, we wanted people to actually explore the data.

With Ignis Atelier, you can adjust oxygen concentration and airflow speed to see how the flame responds. You can explore different presets, compare multiple scenarios side by side, and observe the extinction behaviour recorded in the fabric experiments, where flame extinction occurs around the 2–5 cm/s airflow range under the relevant test conditions.

One thing we particularly cared about was scientific honesty. We haven't used AI to invent missing measurements or generate predictions. The visualisations are based on the experimental data we collected from the published research. Our Sources & Limits section also explains what the dataset supports and where its limitations begin.

We know that combustion science can feel complicated, especially for someone encountering microgravity experiments for the first time. That's why we focused on making the experience interactive, understandable, and accessible to students, teachers, and anyone curious about fire safety in space.

The entire project runs directly in your browser through Vercel, so there's no software to install.

For us, Ignis Atelier is more than just a data visualisation project. It's our attempt to take real space research and turn it into something people can explore, question, and learn from.

Throughout development, we kept three things at the centre of our work: scientific accuracy, a clear user experience, and transparency about what the data can and cannot tell us.
